prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 regime

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the clearest recent case of a new measurement capability that changed what can be done in physics. The magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while thousands of atoms are interrogated at once, and this took optical frequency standards to instabilities and uncertainties near 1e-18. That is an experimentally demonstrated result, not only a proposal: independent clocks at RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, SYRTE, NIST and elsewhere have been compared over fibre and free space, and they agree. The consequences are concrete: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on drifting constants and dark-matter couplings, chronometric geodesy, and the pending redefinition of the second. The credit is also unusually compact. Katori made the proposal and the first Sr demonstrations, and Ye's group pushed the accuracy, stability and many-body clock physics to the frontier. Because the work is distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize, I see no overlap problem and no need for a third name. I propose it as a single-achievement prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and novelty. Hall and Hansch (2005) and Wineland (2012) already cover the comb and the single-ion clock, so some will see the lattice clock as an incremental step in a metrology story the prize has already told twice. The second concern is that many groups made decisive contributions to the 1e-18 performance (Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE teams), and a two-person credit can look arbitrary. A further point is that the practical payoff, the SI redefinition and routine geodetic use, is still pending, so a sceptic may call it a technology milestone more than a discovery about nature. I think the first two points are real but manageable, and the third is weaker than it seems because the measurements already constrain physics.

responses.point: Pearce ranked IceCube first as a new observational window built on a detector concept, and put the lattice-clock pairing second as a clean, mature and well-reproduced allocation.
responses.response: I agree with the instrument-first criterion and think the lattice clock meets it as well as IceCube. The difference for me is attribution and evidence. The clock comparisons are repeated across many independent labs at 1e-18, so the claim has been tested quantitatively. IceCube's central result is firm, but the allocation to Halzen and Spiering sits against a very large collaboration and unresolved AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND precedence. I would put the clock first, with IceCube as a serious later candidate. I would not join it to the clock as a second part, since a two-part prize here would dilute a clean single credit.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked topological insulators first for a simple mechanism with broad consequences and a decisive experimental realisation, and ranked lattice clocks eighth, saying timing is reasonable but not urgent.
responses.response: I take the point that the Z2 classification is conceptually deep and has spread across platforms, but I disagree that the clock is less urgent. Redefinition of the second is a near-term decision, and the lattice clock is the technology that sets it. I also see a bigger attribution problem in B007 than Mehlig does. As he notes, the credit leaves out Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu, and the 2016 prize already covers topological phases. Molenkamp's HgTe measurement is a decisive experiment, so I keep B007 as an alternative, but it is not my first choice while the allocation is disputed.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked lattice clocks first and optical-lattice quantum simulation second, calling the lattice-clock pair a natural, fair pairing and stressing that theory and experiment agree.
responses.response: I agree on the clock. On B010 I am more cautious than her second place suggests. I ranked it seventh because the four-name credit exceeds the three-laureate limit, and a choice between Greiner and Esslinger or leaving out Zoller is a real allocation problem. The quantitative payoff, solving the 2D Fermi-Hubbard phase diagram, is still developing, and the 2001 BEC prize covers much of the cooling toolbox. I would keep it as an alternative, not as a partner to the clock. Since she has atomic-physics expertise here, I would like her view on whether Zoller's theory is essential to the credit.

responses.point: Johansson also ranked lattice clocks first, and noted that other groups (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow) belong to the broader story but are not in the credited list.
responses.response: I agree, and that is the right reason to keep the prize to two names and to word the citation around the invention and realisation of the lattice clock rather than the broad clock field. Johansson ranked cavity optomechanics eighth, while I put it fifth. We differ on where it belongs, but we share the concern that its scope is hard to define across optical, microwave and phononic platforms, so I do not push it as an alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes.

Whether a two-person credit is defensible given the contributions of Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, and whether Katori's role as originator versus Ye's role as record-holder needs explicit wording in the citation.
How much the pending redefinition of the second should weigh in timing, since it is a decision outside the physics itself.
For B007 as an alternative, whether the omission of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu from the credited names can be resolved.
statement.conflict_note: No decisive conflict. Two connections are worth flagging: I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my PhD, and Jun Ye is associated with Hall's JILA environment (from general knowledge, not from my profile), though I have not collaborated with Ye or Katori. I am also on the executive management team of WACQT, which overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, Johansson's home. Neither seems to require recusal, but the committee may wish to note them.
